subject: botany_2
question_text: Give a brief account of pest resistant plants.

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.36, printed question 48. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK NOTE: the guide spells the nematode "Meloidegyne incognitia". The correct name is MELOIDOGYNE INCOGNITA.

insider_note: This answer is really about RNA interference. Getting to double stranded RNA and gene silencing is where three of the four marks are.

steps.label: The problem
steps.margin_note: The parasite, the host, the part attacked, and the loss.
lines: A nematode parasite, MELOIDOGYNE INCOGNITA,
infects the ROOTS of tobacco plants.
The infestation greatly reduces the yield of
tobacco.
Pest resistant plants are developed by
biotechnology to stop this.
steps.why: A root parasite cannot be reached by spraying, so a solution built into the plant is the only practical one.
common_mistakes: Saying the nematode attacks the leaves. It infects the ROOTS.
Misspelling the name. It is Meloidogyne incognita; the guide misprints it.
steps.memory_tip: A root parasite that spraying cannot reach.

steps.label: RNA interference
steps.margin_note: Expand RNAi, say it is natural, and name the double stranded trigger.
lines: The strategy adopted is RNA INTERFERENCE
(RNAi). RNAi is a method of CELLULAR DEFENCE
found in all eukaryotic organisms.
It works by SILENCING a specific mRNA, so that
mRNA is never translated into protein.
The silencing is triggered by DOUBLE STRANDED
RNA.
steps.why: A cell that meets double stranded RNA treats it as a sign of viral infection, and RNAi is the defence it already has — the technique borrows it.
common_mistakes: Saying RNAi cuts DNA. It silences mRNA; the DNA is untouched.
Saying RNAi is artificial. It is a NATURAL cellular defence that is being used.
steps.memory_tip: Silence the message and the protein is never made.

steps.label: Making the transgenic plant
steps.margin_note: The vector, the transgenic plant, and both RNAs. Three numbered steps.
lines: 1. Nematode specific genes are introduced into
the tobacco plant, using AGROBACTERIUM as the
vector.
2. The host tobacco plant is now a TRANSGENIC
plant.
3. The introduced DNA is designed so that BOTH
a SENSE RNA and an ANTI-SENSE RNA are
produced in the host cells.
steps.why: Making both strands in the same cell is what allows them to pair, and the pairing is what triggers the whole defence.
common_mistakes: Saying only one RNA is made. BOTH sense and anti-sense are produced.
Naming the wrong vector. Agrobacterium is the standard plant vector.
steps.memory_tip: Two RNAs made in the same cell, so they can find each other.

steps.label: How the parasite is defeated
steps.margin_note: The pairing, the silencing, and the consequence. Four numbered steps.

lines.text: The parasite's own mRNA is silenced inside

lines: 4. The two RNAs are COMPLEMENTARY, so they
pair and form a DOUBLE STRANDED RNA.
5. This initiates RNAi and silences the specific
nematode mRNA.
6. The parasite can no longer make the protein
it needs, so it cannot survive in the
transgenic plant.
7. The plant is therefore protected.
steps.why: The plant is not made poisonous; it simply switches off a gene the parasite cannot do without, which is why nothing else is harmed.
common_mistakes: Saying the plant poisons the nematode. It SILENCES a nematode gene.
Stopping at 'RNAi happens'. The consequence for the parasite is the last mark.
steps.memory_tip: The plant does not kill it; it just switches off a gene it needs.
